newsitem.title: UK: London stocks start 1997 on a sour note.
newsitem.headline: London stocks start 1997 on a sour note.

text.p: British shares suffered a dismal start to the New Year on Thursday, ending sharply lower after fresh U.S. economic data strengthened fears of inflationary pressures and spooked financial markets.

London's FTSE 100 index of leading shares lost 61.1 points, or 1.5 percent, to close at 4,057.4, after U.S. bond and stock markets reacted violently to signs of stronger than expected manufacturing activity.
Trade remained subdued, however, with many investors taking extended New Year holidays and as a result dealers said slim volumes had exaggerated share price movements.
Losses were broadly based and only a handful of stocks managed to stay in positive territory.
The Mid-250 index fared better though, shedding just 0.47 percent or 21 points to 4,469.4.
The market had made a poor start to the morning as it responded to sharp losses in the U.S. on Tuesday, after the London markets had already closed for the New Year holiday.

After clawing back the bulk of initial losses to reach a day's best of 4,095.3, the FTSE index turned lower once again when Wall Street was surprised by fresh evidence that the U.S. economy was growing strongly.
Sentiment remained gloomy following the news that U.S. manufacturing activity had picked up in December.
"It's not a good start to the New Year," said one trader. "We're at the mercy of Wall Street and the U.S. is only as good as its last data."

Investors were uninspired by the latest UK purchasing managers' report which showed manufacturing order books filling up and prices dropping. Traders said attention was firmly fixed on the U.S. and the possibility of a February rate hike there.
The Dow, which plunged 1.5 percent in the previous session, had added another 60 points to the loss by the time the London markets closed.
"UK shares are more sensitive to U.S. rates than to UK rates," said Robert Buckland, equity strategist at investment bank HSBC James Capel.
"I think we'll have a bumpy ride in the first quarter, but more because of rates in the United States than because of the political noise the UK elections will provide."

However, technical analysts watching market charts said today's setback was merely a correction in a longer term bull run and most saw the FTSE able to reach new heights during the first quarter of 1997.
Shares had set a record close of 4,118.5 on the last trading day of 1996.
